source: MAFF/JICA APPP (Agricultural Productivity Promotion Project in West Tonle Sap) Farmer Field School Technical Manual for Extension Officers, December 2014 -- no elibrary URL visible on this scan.
province: Battambang, Pursat, Kampong Chhnang (APPP project area)
text: In the final weeks before harvest, it is worth walking the field to observe what worked well and what did not, so lessons can be applied to the next planting season. Points worth checking include: whether the actual crop looks close to the expected yield, whether weeds were controlled effectively, whether any off-type or mixed varieties (ពូជលាយ) appeared in the field, how much lodging (ស្រូវដួលដើម) occurred and whether it is likely to affect yield or grain quality, and whether any disease symptoms appeared and how they were, or should be, managed. A simple field method for estimating expected yield before harvest uses small sample quadrats: mark out at least a few 1m x 1m sample squares scattered across the field (representative of different areas, not just the best-looking spot), then for each square count the number of hills, the average number of productive tillers/panicles per hill, and the average number of grains per panicle from a small hand-threshed sample. A rough estimate of the share of filled grain (often assumed around 80% unless visibly worse), combined with an approximate 1,000-grain weight (roughly 30 g for common indica rice at about 13% moisture), allows a rough yield calculation: panicles per sq m = hills per sq m x panicles per hill; filled grains per sq m = panicles per sq m x grains per panicle x 0.8; yield in grams per sq m = filled grains per sq m divided by 1000, multiplied by the 1,000-grain weight; yield in kg per hectare = yield in grams per sq m multiplied by 10.
caveat: These are illustrative field-estimation figures from a training scan, useful for a rough sense of expected yield before harvest (one worked example in the source gave a range of about 4,300-4,800 kg/ha across three sample squares), not a substitute for actual weighed harvest data. The 80% fill-rate and 30 g thousand-grain-weight figures should be adjusted to match the actual variety and field conditions being assessed.
